body:
Why the name Bhaskara needs clarification

The name Bhaskara is associated with 2 important mathematicians and astronomers who lived several centuries apart. Bhaskara I belonged to the 7th century CE and explained and developed Aryabhata's methods. Bhaskara II, also widely known as Bhaskaracharya, belonged to the 12th century CE.

When a question mentions Bhaskara along with the Lilavati or Bijaganita, it is referring to Bhaskara II, not Bhaskara I.

Bhaskara I: commentator on Aryabhata

Bhaskara I lived approximately from 600 CE to 680 CE. He belonged to the mathematical astronomy tradition that developed from Aryabhata's work.

His important writings include:

  • Aryabhatiyabhashya: a commentary on the mathematical portion of Aryabhata's Aryabhatiya, associated with 629 CE.
  • Mahabhaskariya: a treatise on mathematical astronomy.
  • Laghubhaskariya: another astronomical work, shorter than the Mahabhaskariya.

Bhaskara I worked on astronomical calculations and methods involving trigonometric values, including approximations of the sine function. Such calculations were useful for determining celestial positions.

A connection with Gujarat

Bhaskara I's writings refer to places in present-day Gujarat, including Valabhi in Saurashtra and Bharuch. Some scholars have suggested a connection with Saurashtra, but his exact birthplace and movements are not securely established. The references to these places are more certain than a claim that he was born in Gujarat.

Bhaskara II or Bhaskaracharya

Bhaskara II lived approximately from 1114 CE to 1185 CE. He was a major mathematician and astronomer of early medieval India. His best-known major work, the Siddhanta Shiromani, was completed in 1150 CE.

The principal divisions traditionally associated with this work are:

  • Lilavati: arithmetic, measurement and elementary mathematical problems.
  • Bijaganita: algebra and the solution of equations.
  • Grahaganita: mathematical calculations concerning planets.
  • Goladhyaya: the celestial sphere and related astronomical concepts.

The Lilavati and Bijaganita are also commonly treated as separately titled mathematical works. In traditional descriptions of the broader Siddhanta Shiromani, they are grouped with the astronomical divisions.

Distinguishing the contributions

ScholarPeriodWork to remember
Bhaskara I7th century CEAryabhatiyabhashya; Mahabhaskariya
Bhaskara II12th century CELilavati; Bijaganita; Siddhanta Shiromani

The most important distinction is chronological as well as textual. Bhaskara I commented on Aryabhata's 5th-century work; Bhaskara II wrote major mathematical treatises several centuries later.

Prelims focus

  • Bhaskara I: 7th-century mathematician and astronomer.
  • Aryabhatiyabhashya: commentary associated with 629 CE.
  • Bhaskara II or Bhaskaracharya: 1114–1185 CE.
  • Siddhanta Shiromani: completed in 1150 CE.
  • Lilavati: arithmetic; Bijaganita: algebra.
  • Trap: Do not assign the Lilavati to Bhaskara I.

[Sources: University of St Andrews, MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Bhaskara I' and 'Bhaskara II', sections on their writings and dates, consulted 18 November 2026; Uttarakhand Open University, 'Lilavati (Bhaskara II Book)', introductory lecture material, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The principal mathematical and astronomical divisions associated with Bhaskara II.

title: Bhaskara I and Bhaskara II: Different Scholars, Different Works

body:
Ayurveda as an ancient medical tradition

Ayurveda is a system of medical knowledge that developed in ancient India. Its historical literature discusses health, illness, diagnosis, treatment, diet, medicines and surgical procedures.

Two especially important names associated with classical Ayurvedic texts are Charaka and Sushruta. Both are connected with medicine, but their principal texts have different areas of emphasis.

Charaka and the Charaka Samhita

Charaka is associated with the Charaka Samhita, an important Sanskrit medical compendium. NCERT places Charaka approximately in the 1st–2nd centuries CE, although the history of the text includes earlier material and later revisions.

The principal emphasis of the Charaka Samhita is the medical management of disease, commonly associated with kayachikitsa, or internal medicine.

Its subjects include:

  • Recognition and assessment of diseases.
  • Descriptions of bodily functions and states of health.
  • Use of medicines and therapeutic measures.
  • Diet, daily habits and measures intended to preserve health.

For a preliminary examination, the important association is Charaka Samhita — medicine and treatment of disease.

Sushruta and the Sushruta Samhita

Sushruta is associated with the Sushruta Samhita, a foundational work in the history of Indian surgery. The text gives considerable attention to shalya tantra, the surgical branch of Ayurveda.

The subjects discussed in the surgical tradition include:

  • Knowledge of the structure of the human body.
  • Descriptions and uses of surgical instruments.
  • Management of wounds and injuries.
  • Methods of incision, extraction, suturing and other procedures.
  • Reconstructive procedures, including methods associated with the repair of the nose.

The central association for examination purposes is Sushruta Samhita — surgery, surgical instruments and anatomy.

Why the date of Sushruta requires care

Sushruta's exact lifetime is not securely established. The NCERT account associates him with approximately the 4th century CE, while other historical interpretations place the origins of the Sushruta tradition considerably earlier, sometimes around the 6th century BCE. The surviving text developed through revisions over time.

The association between Sushruta and surgery is much more secure for a basic matching question than a single exact birth or death date. Do not treat a disputed date as an established historical certainty.

Charaka and Sushruta compared

ScholarPrincipal textMain emphasis
CharakaCharaka SamhitaInternal medicine, diseases, medicines and diet
SushrutaSushruta SamhitaSurgery, instruments, anatomy and wound care

The difference is one of primary emphasis, not an absolute separation. Both works belong to the broader Ayurvedic tradition, and their subjects can overlap. They are historical medical texts; descriptions of ancient practices should not automatically be taken as evidence that every treatment meets modern standards of clinical safety or effectiveness.

Prelims focus

  • Charaka: associated with the Charaka Samhita.
  • Main field of Charaka Samhita: medicine and treatment of disease.
  • Charaka's textbook period: approximately 1st–2nd centuries CE.
  • Sushruta: associated with the Sushruta Samhita.
  • Main field of Sushruta Samhita: surgery and surgical instruments.
  • Trap: Do not interchange the principal texts of Charaka and Sushruta.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts–I, chapter 'Buildings, Paintings and Books', printed p. 131; 'Anatomy in Ancient India: A Focus on the Susruta Samhita', Journal of Anatomy, 2010, sections on Susruta and the surgical tradition, consulted 18 November 2026; National Centre of Indian Medical Heritage, Journal of Indian Medical Heritage, special edition 2017–2020, 'Biography of Acarya Susruta and His Contribution', section on chronology.]

title: Charaka and Sushruta: Medicine and Surgery in Ancient India

body:
What is metallurgy?

Metallurgy is the knowledge and practice of obtaining metals from their ores, preparing and refining them, combining metals into alloys, and shaping them into useful objects.

Ancient Indian metalworkers developed practical skills in working with copper, bronze and iron. Their achievements can be understood through surviving objects and the techniques used to make them.

Copper, bronze and iron

Craftspeople of the Harappan civilisation used copper and manufactured bronze, an alloy commonly made by combining copper and tin. An alloy is a material formed by combining 2 or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal, to obtain useful properties, such as greater hardness or suitability for casting.

Bronze could be shaped into tools, vessels, ornaments and images. Ironworking later became increasingly important for tools, implements and large forged objects.

The important distinction is that bronze is an alloy, whereas iron is a metal. Bronze production and iron forging involve different materials and techniques.

The Iron Pillar of Delhi

The Iron Pillar at Mehrauli, Delhi, is a notable example of ancient Indian ironworking. The pillar is approximately 7.2 m high and is generally associated with the Gupta period.

Its inscription mentions a ruler named Chandra, commonly identified with Chandragupta II, although the identification is not entirely certain.

The pillar is particularly famous for its remarkable resistance to corrosion over many centuries. Its survival reflects sophisticated ancient ironworking and the properties of the material. It is more accurate to describe the pillar as highly corrosion-resistant than to claim that iron can never corrode.

The Iron Pillar at Mehrauli is an example of iron metallurgy. It is not a bronze object, and it is located in Delhi, not Gujarat.

Bronze casting and the Akota finds in Gujarat

An important Gujarat connection is the discovery of bronze images at Akota, near Vadodara. These finds demonstrate that skilled bronze casting was practised in Gujarat and western India between approximately the 6th and 9th centuries CE.

Many of the Akota bronzes represent Jain Tirthankaras, including Adinath, Parshvanath and Mahavira. Their manufacture required specialised knowledge of modelling and metal casting.

The lost-wax casting method

The lost-wax method is a technique for producing a metal object from a model originally shaped in wax. The basic sequence is:

  1. A model of the intended object is prepared in wax.
  2. The wax model is covered with a suitable moulding material, such as clay.
  3. Heating melts and removes the wax, leaving a cavity of the required shape.
  4. Molten metal is introduced into the mould and allowed to solidify.
  5. The mould is removed and the metal object is finished.

The technique was known in the Indian subcontinent from the period of the Indus civilisation and continued to be used in later periods. It was important in the production of metal images and other objects.

Nagarjuna and the tradition of alchemy

The name Nagarjuna is also associated with the history of Indian alchemy and rasashastra, a tradition concerned with the processing of metals, minerals and substances such as mercury.

Alchemical writings discuss methods for treating, purifying and combining substances. Some also describe attempts to transform base metals into precious metals or to prepare special medicinal substances. These aims belong to the history of alchemy and do not establish that the claimed transformations were successfully achieved.

The work Rasendramangala is associated with an alchemical author called Nagarjuna Siddha, but its precise date remains uncertain.

Distinguishing historical figures and texts

More than one historical or traditional figure bears the name Nagarjuna. The Buddhist philosopher Nagarjuna, usually placed around the 2nd–3rd centuries CE, should not automatically be identified with the author associated with medieval alchemical writings.

The title Rasaratnakara is often attributed to Nagarjuna in popular accounts. Specialist research distinguishes the Rasendramangala associated with Nagarjuna Siddha from the Rasaratnakara attributed to Nityanatha Siddha. The attribution to Nagarjuna should therefore not be presented as an undisputed fact.

Chronology and principal associations at a glance

The major figures belong to different periods and fields. Baudhayana is associated with early geometric rules around 800–500 BCE. Charaka belongs conventionally to the early centuries CE, while the dating of Sushruta is disputed. Aryabhata completed the Aryabhatiya in 499 CE. Varahamihira worked in the 6th century CE. Brahmagupta composed the Brahmasphutasiddhanta in 628 CE, and Bhaskara I wrote his commentary on Aryabhata around 629 CE. Bhaskara II completed the Siddhanta Shiromani in 1150 CE. The precise period of the alchemical Nagarjuna remains uncertain.

The overall development shows several connected traditions: practical geometry, arithmetic and mathematical astronomy, medicine and surgery, and metallurgy. These traditions sometimes overlapped, but they are best understood by matching each scholar with the correct work and principal field.

Prelims focus

  • Bronze: an alloy commonly made from copper and tin.
  • Iron Pillar: Mehrauli, Delhi; approximately 7.2 m high; associated with the Gupta period.
  • Akota: near Vadodara, Gujarat; notable for early medieval Jain bronze images.
  • Lost-wax method: produces metal objects using a wax model and mould.
  • Nagarjuna: associated with an alchemical tradition and the Rasendramangala; precise authorship and chronology require qualification.
  • Trap: Do not confuse the Iron Pillar's ironworking with Akota's bronze casting, or treat every text attributed to Nagarjuna as securely his work.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts–I, chapter 'Buildings, Paintings and Books', printed pp. 122 and 131; NCERT, Class 11, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, chapter 7 'Indian Bronze Sculpture', printed pp. 103–105; University of St Andrews, MacTutor History of Mathematics, biographies of Baudhayana, Aryabhata, Varahamihira, Brahmagupta, Bhaskara I and Bhaskara II, consulted 18 November 2026; Dominik Wujastyk, 'An Alchemical Ghost: The Rasaratnakara by Nagarjuna', Ambix, vol. 31, issue 2, 1984, pp. 70–83; Dominik Wujastyk, 'Nagarjuna Siddha: The Kaksaputa of the Rasendramangala', in Indian Alchemy: Sources and Contexts, Oxford University Press, 2025, pp. 86–119, abstract consulted 18 November 2026.]
